strengths: Formulates a conceptually clean and broadly applicable problem setting: minimizing a target loss function with limited/expensive gradient access by leveraging cheap auxiliary gradient evaluations.

Provides a unified convergence analysis for both classical momentum (AuxMom) and momentum-based variance reduction (AuxMVR) under non-convex smooth optimization, clearly highlighting the role of Hessian similarity $\delta$ and noise correlation $\sigma_{f-h}^2$.
Establishes intuitive connections with control variates, DANE, and local-step methods (such as MIME and SVRG).
weaknesses: High algorithmic and theoretical overlap with MIME (Karimireddy et al., 2020a): AuxMom and AuxMVR, along with their Lyapunov-based proof structures (tracking distance moved $\Delta_k$, momentum error $E^t$, and descent lemmas), directly replicate MimeSGDm and MimeMVR. While the framing here is generalized to an auxiliary function $h(x)$, the mathematical machinery and resulting bounds are nearly identical.

Significant gap between theory and motivating applications: The theoretical guarantees strictly depend on uniform spectral-norm Hessian similarity ($\Vert \nabla^2 f(x) - \nabla^2 h(x) \Vert_2 \le \delta$). As the authors acknowledge, this assumption does not hold for the deep learning applications motivating the paper (e.g., contrastive semi-supervised learning, transfer learning, sub-network masking). In those settings, $\delta$ can be as large as $O(L)$, eliminating any theoretical advantage.

Underwhelming and toy-level empirical evaluation: Experiments are restricted to a 1D scalar quadratic, a small MLP on MNIST with artificial perturbations (rotations / label flipping), and a small tabular logistic regression dataset (Mushrooms). None of the compelling real-world applications discussed in Section 5 (e.g., self-supervised pretraining + fine-tuning, large-scale coresets, model compression) are evaluated against established domain-specific baselines.

Draft incompleteness and numerous presentation issues: Appendix A contains an unfinished placeholder ('The code for our experiments is available at'); multiple citations use authors' first names instead of last names (e.g., 'Baifeng et al.', 'Aviv et al.', 'Xingyu et al.', 'Jingzhao et al.', 'Lihua et al.'); and frequent grammatical issues and informal phrasing occur throughout the text.

For decentralized helpers with $S > 1$, the convergence proof relies on Assumption C.17 ($\delta$-weak convexity of $f$), which becomes unnaturally restrictive as the dissimilarity $\delta \to 0$, revealing a technical limitation in the current aggregation analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses a very natural and practically relevant problem: how to leverage a cheap or abundant auxiliary loss function to accelerate the optimization of an expensive target objective.

The conceptual framing using Hessian similarity ($\|\nabla^2 f(x) - \nabla^2 h(x)\|_2 \le \delta$) provides an appealing, general perspective that does not require the global minimizers of the target and auxiliary objectives to coincide.

The theoretical analysis is fairly comprehensive, analyzing both standard momentum (AuxMom) and momentum-based variance reduction (AuxMVR) in the non-convex stochastic setting, complete with explicit convergence rates showing how small $\delta$ and correlated noise improve the bounds.
Theorem 4.2 provides a helpful counterexample and lower bound formalizing why the naive alternation between target and auxiliary gradients inevitably suffers from gradient bias.
weaknesses: Technical and conceptual novelty relative to MIME (Karimireddy et al., 2020a) appears limited. The algorithmic template (using local steps with a momentum-based gradient difference correction) and the proof architecture (bounding inner-step displacement $\Delta_k^t$, momentum error $E^t$, and constructing a Lyapunov function) are essentially direct adaptations of MIME/MVR to the two-function setting.

The empirical evaluation is very rudimentary and falls short of validating the ambitious scope claimed in the paper. Despite motivating the framework with federated learning, transfer learning, semi-supervised contrastive learning, and compressed model training (Section 5), the experiments only evaluate a 1D scalar quadratic toy problem, a tiny feedforward MLP on rotated/corrupted MNIST, and logistic regression on the small 'mushrooms' dataset.

The manuscript suffers from severe presentation issues, typographical errors, and unfinished sentences throughout: (i) In Section 1 / Related Work, multiple citations use first names rather than last names due to misformatted BibTeX entries (e.g., 'Baifeng et al.', 'Aviv et al.', 'Xingyu et al.', 'Jingzhao et al.', 'Lihua et al.'); (ii) Section 4.1 ends abruptly with an incomplete sentence: 'Hence approaches that try to reduce it like (Karimireddy et al., 2020b;a)'; (iii) In Section 4.2 (page 7), a sentence ends prematurely: '...this is the case in general if $\delta/L, \sigma_h^2/\sigma_f^2$ are small and $\sigma_{f-h}^2/\sigma_f^2$.'; (iv) Appendix A literally states 'The code for our experiments is available at ' with a blank space and no URL.

In the decentralized setting with multiple helpers ($S > 1$), the analysis requires an additional weak-convexity assumption (Assumption C.17), which requires $f(x) + \delta \|x\|^2$ to be convex. When $\delta$ is small (the very regime where auxiliary information is informative and useful), this assumption becomes almost equivalent to demanding standard convexity, which severely restricts the claimed non-convex scope.

The step sizes and momentum parameters analyzed in Theorems 4.3 and 4.5 depend on unknown problem constants (such as $\delta$, $L$, and noise variances) and require conservative conditions (e.g., $\eta \le 1/(192\delta K)$), with little guidance provided on how these hyperparameters can be adaptively tuned in practice without knowledge of $\delta$.

strengths: Unifying Conceptual Framework: The paper provides a clear and principled optimization formulation for leveraging cheap/available auxiliary objective functions $h(x)$ to accelerate the minimization of an expensive target objective $f(x)$, drawing connections across federated learning, batch reuse, and semi-supervised learning.

Theoretical Analysis: The paper provides non-convex convergence analyses for both momentum (AuxMom) and momentum-based variance reduction (AuxMVR) under Hessian similarity ($\|\nabla^2 f(x) - \nabla^2 h(x)\| \le \delta$). The resulting bounds quantify how local steps $K$, similarity $\delta$, and correlated noise $\sigma_{f-h}^2$ impact convergence.

Clear Motivation for Bias Correction: The lower bound in Theorem 4.2 cleanly illustrates why naive alternating/proxy optimization suffers from irreducible asymptotic bias $\Omega(\zeta^2)$ when gradient bias is present, motivating the momentum-based correction.
weaknesses: Limited Algorithmic and Proof Novelty over MIME: The core algorithmic idea—correcting local helper updates using a momentum buffer that tracks $\nabla f - \nabla h$—is essentially an adaptation of the MIME framework (Karimireddy et al., 2020a) and STORM/MVR (Cutkosky & Orabona, 2019). The mathematical tools and proof structure closely mirror these existing works.

Gap Between Theory and Practical Applications: A central assumption across the theoretical results is uniform Hessian similarity $\|\nabla^2 f(x) - \nabla^2 h(x)\|_2 \le \delta$. As the authors acknowledge in Section 5, this assumption rarely holds for the motivating applications (e.g., deep networks with ReLU activations, contrastive self-supervised learning, or transfer learning across different loss landscapes), creating a noticeable disconnect between the theory and the pitched use cases.

Weak and Toy Empirical Validation: The empirical evaluation is restricted to a 1D scalar toy problem, a small 3-layer MLP on MNIST with synthetic perturbations (rotated images or randomly flipped labels), and logistic regression on the small UCI Mushrooms dataset (8,124 samples). None of the compelling practical applications mentioned in Section 5 (e.g., large-scale pre-training/transfer learning, contrastive SSL, or compressed/masked neural network training) are evaluated on standard benchmarks.

Incomplete Details and Missing Information: In Appendix A, the manuscript states 'The code for our experiments is available at' but leaves the URL completely blank. Additionally, several citations are improperly formatted or malformed (e.g., '(Baifeng et al.; Aviv et al.; Xingyu et al.)' on page 2, 'Jingzhao et al.' on page 5, 'SCSG(Lihua et al.)' on page 13).

strengths: The paper proposes a unified optimization abstraction for minimizing a target function $f(x)$ using cheap/available auxiliary information from a side function $h(x)$, capturing multiple settings (e.g., coreset training, semi-supervised learning, transfer learning, and federated learning).

Convergence guarantees are provided for both classical momentum (AuxMOM) and momentum-based variance reduction (AuxMVR) in the smooth non-convex setting, showing how the complexity bounds depend on the Hessian dissimilarity $\delta$ and variance $\sigma_{f-h}^2$ rather than the full target Lipschitz constant and variance.
The paper provides an extensive appendix with detailed step-by-step proofs for the main convergence theorems, as well as extensions to decentralized helpers.
weaknesses: Novelty and differentiation from MIME: The algorithmic framework (using momentum on $f - h$ combined with local steps on $h$) is virtually identical to the Mime framework (Karimireddy et al., 2020a, MimeSGDm and MimeMVR). While the authors note this connection, the technical contribution over Mime is narrow; the analysis heavily mirrors Mime's proof strategy under the exact same Hessian similarity assumption.

Mismatch between motivating applications and theoretical assumptions: A central motivation of the paper is applying this framework to transfer learning, masked models, and contrastive semi-supervised learning. However, as acknowledged in Section 5, Hessian similarity does not hold in these neural network regimes. The theory is thus detached from the main practical motivations, holding rigorously only for simple models like linear/logistic regression.

Empirical evaluation is weak and relies on toy models: The deep learning experiments are confined to small MLPs on MNIST and a tiny 2-convolution network on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 achieving very low test accuracies (~55% on CIFAR-10, ~25% on CIFAR-100). Furthermore, comparisons primarily plot metrics against iterations or stochastic gradients of $f$, while omitting wall-clock time and full compute/FLOP costs incurred by the $K$ inner steps of $h$.

Presentation and citation quality issues: Several references are severely malformed, citing first names as last names (e.g., 'Baifeng et al.', 'Aviv et al.', 'Xingyu et al.' on page 2; 'Jingzhao et al.' on page 6; 'Lihua et al.' on page 15). Additionally, Appendix A ('Code') is left completely empty without an actual link or description.

strengths: Conceptual unification: Formulating diverse machine learning paradigms (coreset training, transfer learning, federated learning, and semi-supervised learning) under the umbrella of stochastic optimization with auxiliary information is an interesting and unifying perspective.

Theoretical development: The paper establishes rigorous convergence rates for both classical momentum (AuxMOM) and momentum-based variance reduction (AuxMVR) under Hessian similarity, explicitly characterizing the complexity reduction for the target function $f$ when $\delta \ll L$ or $\sigma_{f-h}^2 \ll \sigma_f^2$.
Detailed appendix: The manuscript provides step-by-step proofs for the main convergence theorems (e.g., Lemma C.5 through Lemma C.9 and the decentralized extensions in Appendix C.4).
weaknesses: High overlap with prior work: The core algorithmic scheme and proof architecture (specifically tracking gradient discrepancies via momentum/control variates under Hessian similarity) bear extensive similarities to MIME (Karimireddy et al., 2020a) and SCAFFOLD (Karimireddy et al., 2020b). The conceptual jump from federated local client functions to a generic auxiliary function $h$ is natural, but the technical algorithmic novelty relative to MIME is somewhat limited.

Restrictive nature of Hessian similarity: As acknowledged honestly in Section 5, Hessian similarity rarely holds in deep learning tasks, non-smooth architectures (e.g., ReLUs), or drastic domain-shift / transfer-learning setups. While logistic regression is an exception, the applicability of the theoretical bounds to the paper's primary deep learning motivations remains questionable.

Preliminary experimental evaluation: The empirical validation relies on relatively toy setups (simple MLPs and small CNNs on MNIST and CIFAR with random sub-sampling or uniform rotations). Standard benchmark comparisons in transfer learning, actual coreset selection algorithms (rather than uniform downsampling), or competitive semi-supervised methods are missing.

Presentation and completeness issues: Appendix A ('The code for our experiments is available at') is left completely blank without a repository link. Additionally, several citations in the body text are improperly formatted (e.g., 'SCSG(Lihua et al.)', 'Baifeng et al.; Aviv et al.; Xingyu et al.').

strengths: Unifying perspective: The paper formulates an intuitive general framework for stochastic optimization with auxiliary information, connecting disparate paradigms such as federated learning, transfer learning, coreset training, and semi-supervised learning under a single optimization lens.

Theoretical guarantees under Hessian similarity: The authors provide non-convex convergence rates for two algorithmic variants (AuxMOM using classical momentum and AuxMVR using momentum-based variance reduction), showing how the dependence on the Lipschitz constant and variance can be shifted from $L, \sigma_f^2$ to $\delta, \sigma_{f-h}^2$.

Interesting analytical observations: The observation that binary logistic regression possesses a Hessian independent of class labels provides an interesting and concrete example where the $\delta = 0$ Hessian similarity condition strictly holds for unlabeled data.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work: The algorithmic design (combining local steps with a momentum-based gradient correction between a local and global proxy) and analysis heavily mirror existing techniques developed in federated learning, specifically MIME (Karimireddy et al., 2020a) and MVR/STORM (Cutkosky & Orabona, 2019). The core contribution is largely an abstract reframing of the MIME algorithmic mechanism to auxiliary functions.

Fundamental gap between theory and practical applications: The theoretical guarantees rely strictly on bounded Hessian dissimilarity ($\|\nabla^2 f(x) - \nabla^2 h(x)\|_2 \le \delta$). However, as the authors concede in Section 5, this assumption fails to hold in nearly all deep learning motivating applications (rotated images, neural network compression/masks, transfer learning across domains). Consequently, the theory does not actually explain the empirical behavior in these settings.

Weak and unconvincing empirical evaluation: The deep learning experiments are conducted on toy setups (e.g., an MLP on MNIST, or a tiny CNN on CIFAR reaching only ~55% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 and ~20% on CIFAR-100). Furthermore, the evaluation lacks established domain-specific baselines (e.g., standard semi-supervised learning, domain adaptation, or modern coreset selection methods), reports no error bars or standard deviations across random seeds, and provides no wall-clock time comparisons to substantiate practical computational gains.

Clarity and presentation deficiencies: The manuscript contains multiple rough edges and drafting errors, including malformed citations without years (e.g., 'Baifeng et al.; Aviv et al.; Xingyu et al.' on page 2, 'Jingzhao et al.' on page 6, 'SCSG(Lihua et al.)' on page 15), stray notation/copy-paste artifacts in algorithm pseudocode (e.g., '§ momentum' in Algorithms 1, 3, and 5), and an incomplete sentence in Appendix A ('The code for our experiments is available at ').
